newsitem.title: TURKEY: Soccer-Turkey's fallen star acts out his true story.
newsitem.headline: Soccer-Turkey's fallen star acts out his true story.

text.p: Once hailed as Turkey's best soccer player but then disgraced by smuggling charges and an adulterous affair, Tanju Colak set out on Tuesday to put the record straight by playing himself in a television series.

"The Life of the King", a 13-part series, takes the viewers through the life of Colak, offering insights into memorable moments from before he was born to his imprisonment for two years in 1994 for car smuggling.

"We decided with Tanju a long time ago that we wanted to do this," producer-director Gursel Aksun told Reuters. "He told us the whole story -- we told him to give it to us straight, with no bias or anything. And that was what he wanted too."
Why Tanju felt the need to do this is clear from the start, when young son Anil asks his mother: "Why don't the television people like my dad? They keep making him out to be a bad man."

The 33-year-old ex-European Golden Boot winner, known simply as "Tanju" and dubbed "the King" in Turkey, was rarely out of the headlines in the late 1980s for his soccer prowess when he played for Black Sea team Samsunspor and Istanbul's Galatasaray.
In the 1990s he was pursued by a completely different pack of journalists, probing into every detail of a turbulent three-year affair with a haughty film star, and his court case.
The series opened in July 1994, with Tanju in Macedonian capital Skopje to play for a "rest of the world" team against Russia.
His wife, Aysu has a nightmare and predicts "bad things are going to happen" -- cue dramatic music.
Swiftly a warrant is issued for Tanju's arrest, Interpol alerted and journalists begin to patrol his house and claim some mafioso-type deal was struck to ensure his eventual acquittal.
More forebodings and predictions in flashbacks to Tanju's humble origins in the Black Sea town of Samsun follow:
His father says he will have a son who will became a famous soccer player after his mother says the unborn baby is kicking her stomach. The boy is named Tanju after a soccer player.
Tanju's grandfather predicts the name will mean trouble for the boy because it is not a traditional Moslem name with origins in the Koran or the life of the prophet Mohammed.
What form this trouble may take is hinted at when the little Tanju, playing in the clapped-out family car in Samsun, promises to get his father a wonderful new car when he is famous.
Tanju's film star lover is portrayed as a figure from a well-forgotten past. The pair split up in 1992.
"Tanju is happy with the way it turned out," Aksun said.
While in jail, Tanju appeared in a chocolate spread advert set in prison. So is this the start of a new career for Tanju, banned from professional soccer after his conviction?

"Well, it was a real strain for him -- he was no actor and I doubt he understood television even when he was doing the series," Aksun said. "And he said when we finished that he would never do such a thing again."
